$comment: Gzip transfer size on the production build. Routes are DISCOVERED from the
build output, not listed here: a route that must be added by hand is a
route that will eventually be forgotten, and forgotten routes get heavy.
js.shared vs js.route exists because one `js` number conflates the
framework baseline — which we do not write — with our own client code,
which we choose every time. Reported together the framework hides our
growth. Split, the budget binds hardest on the half we control.
js.shared is effectively a tripwire for Next/React upgrades and for code
creeping into every route. js.route is the real allowance for features.
deferred bounds everything no route loads on first paint: a dynamic import
moves weight, it does not remove it, and without a limit 'lazy-loaded'
becomes a place to hide an unbounded bundle.
MOVED 5 KB from js.shared to js.route when the tree went under app/[lang].
The layout holds a Client Component (Nav), and once the layout sits below a
dynamic segment Turbopack stops hoisting it into the chunk every route
shares. Measured before and after: shared 174.8 -> 169.5, route 1.7 -> 6.4,
total 176.5 -> 175.9. Nothing got heavier — the accounting moved — so the
allowance moved with it rather than being raised.
RAISED css 8000 -> 9216 and total 300000 -> 303104 for the interaction layer.
Stated rather than absorbed quietly, because that is the only thing this
file is for. Measured after, not predicted: css 7.24 -> 7.7 KB, total 288.6 -> 289.2 KB
worst route. The additions are 13 distinct effects and
cross-document shared-element transitions, all of it CSS — js.route did not
move. The binding weights are unchanged and are not these: the font is
88 KB and the framework bundle 169.5 KB, together 257 KB of the total.
Reverting is one edit here plus removing styles/interaction.css's last two
sections; nothing else depends on it.
RAISED css 9216 -> 10240. Stated, because that is the only thing this file
is for. The site's entire visual identity is 8.5 KB of gzip CSS and the
limit was set before it published three things it now does: a mark folded
from its own commit record, its own measured weight, and a type scale that
differs by section density. 0.5 KB of headroom is not room to design in.
The font was checked first, because at 88 KB it is 30% of the total and the
obvious suspect. It is not waste: the design uses the wdth axis at BOTH 100
and 125 and four weights (400/500/700/900), measured in styles/*.css, and
eight static instances would be larger than one two-axis variable face.
There is no cheap win there — only a design concession, which is a
different decision from this one.
RAISED /build html to 25600 as a NAMED exception, not a shared raise. Measured
24,842 B on /ko against 24,000. The page had been over the gate at HEAD for some
time before it was noticed, which is worth recording: this gate only runs after a
build, and the route that reports the repository's own health was the one quietly
failing it. Its self-cap (ROW_CHAR_BUDGET, already lowered from 2600 to 1900) is
spent — the remaining weight is the perf table, the phases and the prose, so
lowering the dial again would delete the commit record to pay for something else.
ADDED a named exception for /portfolio/revenue: html 45056, total 323584. It is
the heaviest route on the site by a wide margin — 43.5 KB against the 31.5 KB
districts exception — and the first one whose weight is not a map. Nine figures
and 617 table cells is what a dashboard costs; the exception is named rather
than the shared budget being raised, so no other route inherits the room.
`total` was deliberately NOT raised. /ko/build sits at 292.5 KB of 296 and
the css raise costs it about 0.8 KB, so it still fits. The ceiling stays
where it is and the next thing that wants weight has to argue for itself.
NAMED EXCEPTION for /portfolio/districts instead of a global raise. It was a
global raise for one commit (html 24000 -> 25600) and that was the wrong
shape: the route is the only one of 135 whose content is DATA rather than
prose — 245 districts, each with a name, a grid position, two counts and a
rate — and every kilobyte added to the global ceiling is a kilobyte handed
to 134 prose pages that never asked for it. `overrides` is keyed by the
locale-free path, can only raise a limit, and prints a marked row.
Measured, not predicted — /ko/portfolio/districts, gzip:
as first written, 490 SVG elements          37,632 B html
figure built as strings at build time       25,835 B
integer grid, shorter ids, tighter numbers  24,863 B
retiled onto the country + hover popup      30,310 B   <- shipped
global limit, unchanged                     24,000 B
The first drop is the whole point and is worth writing down: a Server
Component ships its output TWICE — once as HTML to paint and once as a
serialized tree (__next_f) so the client can carry on rendering. Split on
the original page that was 11.6 KB of markup against 26.5 KB of serialized
tree. Nothing on this route is interactive and the table is frozen, so the
second copy was 70% of the page for no purpose. Building the field as three
strings in lib/cartogram.districts.figure.ts makes that copy one string
instead of five hundred objects. There is no API to opt a static subtree out
of the payload, so what remains is inherent.
size encoding, two SVG layers              30,310 B
colour encoding, one layer                 28,497 B
natural breaks, 8 classes, legend counts   29,018 B   <- shipped
The last two steps ADDED capability and one of them REMOVED weight. The
hexagons tile the country's own outline instead of scattering across a
grid; a hover popup carries each district's two raw counts (3,996 B of
`data-n`, of which the population half is 1,621 B — kept, because "622
offices among 274,346 people" is the sentence a rate alone cannot say);
and the value moved from hexagon SIZE to hexagon COLOUR. That last one
collapsed a full-size outline layer and a scaled fill layer into one
element per district and gave 1,813 B back. The exception below came DOWN
from 31,232 B accordingly. A limit that is not re-measured after the page
gets cheaper is not a limit, it is a memory.
What was NOT done to reach the number, with the cost of each measured:
dropping the 245-row rank list would have saved 1,690 B and is the only way
a screen reader gets the values off a map with no labels; dropping the
per-hexagon <title> would have saved 4,585 B and is the whole of the hover
with JavaScript off. Neither is a byte problem, so neither was solved as one.
The last 521 B is prose, not picture: quantile classing put 19.3 and 39.8
in the same colour, and replacing it with Fisher-Jenks meant the page now
has to say why the classes hold 41, 27, 46, 56, 43, 23, 6 and 3 districts
rather than 35 each. A classification a reader cannot check is worse than
a wider budget line.
RAISED css 10240 -> 10752 and total 303104 -> 303616 for a SECOND cartogram.
/portfolio/prices draws price change on the same 245 cells, and its scale
diverges: nine fills instead of eight, in two hues instead of one, plus the
matching legend swatches. Measured, 10,340 B against a 10,240 limit. The css
raise lifts every route's total by the same amount, which is why the total
moved with it and not for a reason of its own — /ko/portfolio/prices came
out at 303,142 B against 303,104.
A CHEAPER FIX WAS TRIED FIRST AND MADE IT WORSE. Each ramp is written twice,
once as `fill` on the cells and once as `background` on the legend swatches,
so both modules were rewritten to declare the nine colours once as custom
properties and reference them from both places. That is 18 `color-mix()`
calls down to 9. It measured 10,445 B — 105 B WORSE. gzip was already
collapsing the repeated `color-mix(in oklab, var(--accent) NN%, var(--ground))`
strings, and replacing them with nine distinct variable names traded
compressible repetition for incompressible novelty. Reverted. The
duplication stays because it is cheaper than the abstraction, which is not
the answer anyone would guess.
RAISED the districts exception and ADDED one for prices, for the 읍면동
drill-down. Clicking a hexagon opens that district's sub-district grid on
the same page. What that cost each map, measured:
data-sgg on 215 of 245 cells             1,643 B
nolink on the 30 with no grid              158 B
the client component (js.route 6.5->7.2)   ~700 B
The five-digit code is the file the page fetches, and 215 distinct codes
are 1.6 KB of pure entropy — an index would only move that table into the
JavaScript. What it BOUGHT is 430 routes not built: all 215 grids inlined
would have been 32.8 KB gzip of markup plus about as much serialized tree,
and one grid on demand is 221 B at the median.
prices gets its own line rather than a global raise for the same reason
districts did: 130 prose routes sit at or under 23.0 KB and the ceiling
should keep binding on them. Two data maps, two named exceptions.
NOT COUNTED BY THIS FILE: public/data/umd/*.json, 215 files and 132,375 B
on disk. The gate measures routes and those are assets, so their weight is
checked by scripts/check-umd.mjs instead. Said out loud because a payload
no gate can see is how a budget stops meaning anything.
The exception is this route's measurement plus 934 B, not an allowance to
grow into, and it leaves the global ceiling where /ko/build (23,210 B) has
always had to live.
RAISED the prices exception 26,624 -> 26,880 B html because THE COUNTRY GOT
BIGGER. 27 시군구 — 광주·전남, 11% of the map and 3.16M residents — had been
fetched under region codes the API retired when the two provinces merged.
data.go.kr answers a retired LAWD_CD with HTTP 200, resultCode 000 and
totalCount 0, which is indistinguishable from a district that filed nothing,
so 648 empty cache files looked like a quiet market and this page published
them in its "표본 부족" class. With the region fetched, measured districts
went 167 -> 179 and the page went 19 B over its own exception. Weight that
arrives because a hole was filled is the one kind this file should never
argue with; scripts/check-coverage.mjs now fails the build on any district
whose whole window is empty, so the next such hole costs a build, not a
budget line.

/build.$why: Measured: html 24,842 B gzip on /ko and 24,815 B on /en, against a 24,000 B budget — over by 842 B, about 3.5%. `total` is 295.3 KB of 303.6 and is NOT raised; only html moves. The ceiling is 25,600 B, which is 758 B of headroom rather than a round-up: the page's own record is capped by ROW_CHAR_BUDGET, so it does not creep, and the next thing that wants room here still has to argue for it.
/build.$whyNotTheDial: app/[lang]/build/page.tsx caps its commit record and the cap has already been spent. Its comment records the history: a row COUNT lowered 90 to 64 to 52 to 38, failing this gate in between, then replaced by a CHARACTER budget because a row's weight is its subject and its links and those vary fourfold. That budget was set at 2600 and is now 1900. Turning it down a third time would strip the commit record — which is the page's whole subject — to pay for weight that is no longer in the commit record. The remainder is the perf table, the phase roster and the prose, none of which has a dial.
/build.$whyNotGlobal: A named exception rather than raising `budgets.html`. Over 130 essay routes fit the 24,000 B budget with room (the eli5 pages run 9 to 17 KB); raising the shared ceiling would hand every one of them a kilobyte nobody asked for, which is the ratchet the note below refuses for `total`.

/portfolio/districts.$why: 245 districts x (name, cell, brokers, population) drawn as a hexagon tiling of the country, the same 245 rows listed again in rank order, and a code per cell for the 읍면동 drill-down. The page IS the data. See the measurements in $comment above.

/portfolio/revenue.$why: Nine figures on one route, and the route IS the figures. Measured, not predicted: html 43.5 KB gzip on /ko, total 316.1 KB. The ceilings are 44 and 318 KB — about a kilobyte and a half of headroom each, which is one more figure, not one more page. What is in it — 36 months of stepped MRR and its movement decomposition, 36 monthly rows in one table, 11 small multiples over 36 points each, the 245-cell district tiling with a title per cell, a 12-quarter cohort triangle drawn twice, 19 quota bars, and a table under every figure because a value reachable only by pointing at a mark is not reachable. About 62% of the raw bytes are the RSC flight payload, which duplicates the markup for client-side navigation and is not something this page chooses.
/portfolio/revenue.$cut: Three things were cut before asking for this exception rather than after. Monthly cohorts became quarterly: 1,433 marks to 257, and the curves went from resting on ~25 accounts each to ~75, so it was a statistics fix that happened to be a weight fix. The MRR panel and the movement panel merged into one, which removed a second copy of the same 36-row table (288 cells) and is the better reading anyway — the columns only argue anything while the line is in view. The cohort cells kept their titles because the table under them holds only each cohort's last column.
/portfolio/revenue.$kept: The 245 titles on the map and the 617 table cells stayed. Both are the page's only non-pointer path to its values, and this site has a text alternative for every figure it has ever shipped.

/portfolio/prices.$why: The same 245-cell tiling under a diverging scale, plus its legend and the drill-down codes. Nine fills in two hues instead of eight in one.
/portfolio/prices.$raised: 26,112 -> 26,624 -> 26,880 B html and 307,712 -> 308,224 -> 309,248 B total, and the last step is 12 more districts holding a value rather than a design that grew. 광주·전남 had been queried under region codes the API retired at the merger, so 27 districts returned zero rows and 12 of them cleared the pair floor once the data arrived. Measured: /ko 26,643 B against 26,624 — over by 19 bytes. The data alone accounts for more than that: the rank list went 7,931 -> 8,492 B raw and 1,375 -> 1,446 B gzip, the 12 cells' data-n grew 19 B and their titles 49 B. The prose was tightened in the same commit and came out roughly neutral, so the overrun is entirely values. The new ceiling is 237 B of headroom on html — about four more districts crossing the floor, not room to design in.
